what_it_does: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) is an alternative AI approach that represents concepts as very long binary strings (hypervectors — vectors of thousands of bits) and classifies inputs by measuring how similar two hypervectors are using cosine similarity (a calculation of the angle between them). HDC is attractive for low-power edge devices because it avoids deep neural networks, but cosine similarity still requires multiplications that are expensive on tiny FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays — chips whose logic can be reconfigured after manufacturing, commonly used in edge devices). Existing binary HDC (using only 0s and 1s) drastically reduces that cost but loses too much accuracy. FATE applies mixed-precision quantization (using smaller/rounded numbers — but crucially, using different numbers of bits for different dimensions of the hypervector depending on how important each dimension is) and also skips zero-valued dimensions altogether (a technique called sparsity — ignoring the unimportant zeros to save computation). The co-design targets resource-constrained FPGAs and, according to the abstract, achieves higher accuracy than binary HDC at lower hardware cost than full-precision HDC.
